headline: The Race Runs Hot at 3.6 Knots: Bass Go Deep, Plum Gut Sits on Albie Watch
subhead: Trophy stripers have shoved off into the nighttime program while the Gut waits on the first real push of false albacore.
body_markdown:
Race Rock was reading 3.6 knots on the last big ebb I ran through there, and that number tells you almost everything you need to know about this week. That's strong water for late July — not maximum-spring strong, but strong enough to hold bait hard against the rock and strong enough to keep the bass from showing themselves in daylight. When The Race is running like that with surface temps sitting in the high 60s to low 70s, the fish don't fight the current in the open — they tuck down on the structure and wait for dark.

Kings Point is up at 70.9, New London's holding at 69.4, and that gradient matters. The western Sound is warmer and more mature right now, but out here at the eastern gates, the water's still cool enough on the bottom third of the column to keep big bass comfortable through the day. Problem is, comfortable doesn't mean visible. I've had three trips this week where the sounder showed good marks stacked on the downcurrent side of Valiant Rock in 35 to 50 feet, and daytime presentations — wire line, big bucktails, jigged slow off the bottom — got looked at more than they got hit. Two fish boated Tuesday afternoon, both in the low 30-inch range, both came right at the top of the ebb before the current built past 2 knots. That's the window. Once Race Rock gets past 3 knots at midday, I'm not wasting bucktails on it — I'm coming back at night.

After dark is where this fishery is actually happening right now. Eels drifted on wire through the Race and Plum Gut, bunker chunks soaked on the up-current edge of the Sluiceway on slack tide — that's producing the real fish, 20 to 40 pounds, holding tight to the bottom structure where the thermocline gives them cover from the warm surface layer. If you're going to fish this pattern, know your slack to the minute. Race Rock's slack this week is running roughly 20 to 25 minutes ahead of the printed time at New London — the rock chokes the flow and the water keeps moving after the tide technically turns. Valiant Rock slacks a touch later than Race Rock itself, usually 10 to 15 minutes behind. Miss that window by half an hour in either direction and you're fishing 2-plus knots of water that'll bury your wire line before it ever gets to the fish.

Plum Gut is the one everybody's asking me about, and I'll be straight with you — no confirmed albies or bonito through the Gut yet. We flagged the early scouting window last week, and the water's finally sitting right for it: temps have crossed the threshold at Montauk (69.1) and along the approaches, and the moon's building toward full in early August, which means current through the Gut is only going to get stronger and more concentrated over bait in the next week to ten days. That's exactly the setup that triggers the first real showing. I've got the epoxy jigs rigged and ready — half-ounce and three-quarter-ounce, unpainted and green mackerel pattern — but right now the Gut is still mostly bluefish, and they're not shy about it. Blitzes on bunker schools pushing through on the last two hours of the ebb, cocktail blues to 6 pounds tearing up peanut-sized bait right on the surface off Great Gull Island. If you want fast rod-bending action while we wait on the albies, that's your play — small metal, Deadly Dicks and half-ounce Kastmasters, cast into the froth and retrieved fast.

Fluke have thinned out on the open flats the way they always do once the shallow water heats up, but the inlet-adjacent structure is still working. Drifting the deeper bends off Plum Gut and the edges of the Sluiceway in 25 to 40 feet with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails has been steady if not spectacular — a few keepers to 5 pounds mixed with a lot of shorts, best on the last two hours of the incoming when the moving water pulls bait off the structure. Black sea bass are the one bottom fishery that hasn't skipped a beat all summer — the reef structure around Little Gull and the rock piles off Race Rock are holding good numbers on squid and clam belly in 40 to 60 feet, and that bite doesn't care what the surface temp is doing.

Looking ahead, the moon's waxing toward full over the next week and that's going to push current speeds up through the Race, Plum Gut, and Fishers Island Sound — bigger max flows, but also cleaner, more predictable slack windows once you learn where they shift to. If the pattern holds, I'd expect the nighttime bass bite to stay the most reliable program through early August, and I'd keep a rod rigged for albies every single trip through the Gut from here on — the water's ready, we just need the fish to commit. Best case, they show within the next week while current's building and bait's getting pinned in the rips. If they slide past us into August without showing here, Block Island and the Race approaches would be my next stop to check.
